los.text: Describe how to collect essential history points and to analyse data related to AKI
los.html:
• Definition (KDIGO / NICE NG148): serum creatinine rise ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5 × baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h.
StageCreatinineUrine output
11.5–1.9 × baseline (or ≥26 µmol/L rise)<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
22.0–2.9 × baseline<0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h
3≥3 × baseline, or ≥354 µmol/L, or started on RRT<0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h, or anuria ≥12 h
History
  • Often asymptomatic (found on bloods)
  • Reduced urine output
  • Fluid losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, bleeding, poor intake), sepsis, heart failure
  • Drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics, gentamicin, contrast, lithium, metformin)
  • Obstruction (LUTS, prostate, stones, pelvic cancer)
  • Intrinsic renal clues (haematuria, rash, joint pains, haemoptysis: vasculitis; muscle pain or long lie: rhabdomyolysis; bone pain: myeloma)
  • Uraemic symptoms (nausea, itch, confusion, pericarditis)
  • CKD, baseline creatinine.
Data to analyse
  • Trend vs baseline creatinine (old results)
  • Urine output and fluid balance chart
  • Obs (BP, HR, NEWS2)
  • Weight
  • K⁺ and bicarbonate
  • Urine dipstick (before catheter)
  • Urea:creatinine ratio (high in pre-renal and upper GI bleeding).
CategoryCauses
Pre-renal (most common)Hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis, drugs reducing renal perfusion
Renal (intrinsic)Acute tubular necrosis (prolonged ischaemia, toxins), glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis, rhabdomyolysis, myeloma, HUS
Post-renalStones, prostate enlargement, pelvic tumours, blocked catheter, retroperitoneal fibrosis

los.text: Identify risk factors of acute kidney injury in the acute setting and link them to treatment and preventative strategies.
los.html:
Risk factor (NICE NG148)Linked prevention
Age ≥65Monitor U&E in acute illness
CKD (eGFR <60), previous AKIAvoid nephrotoxins, renal-adjust doses
Heart failure, liver disease, diabetesCareful fluid and drug management
Sepsis, hypovolaemiaEarly fluids, prompt antibiotics
Nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics in hypovolaemia)Review, withhold, monitor levels
Iodinated contrastAssess risk; IV hydration (e.g. sodium chloride 0.9%) for at-risk patients; check creatinine after
Urinary obstructionBladder scan, catheter
Cognitive impairment or dependence (can't drink independently)Fluid charts, support with drinking
Major surgery (especially cardiac or vascular)Peri-operative fluid and drug review
  • "Sick day rules" during dehydrating illness, temporarily stop: Sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, Diuretics, Metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors (SADMANS)
    • restart 24–48 h after eating and drinking normally.

los.text: Describe the pathogenesis of, how to make a diagnosis of and manage Myeloma Kidney
los.html:
Myeloma kidney (cast nephropathy)
  • Clonal plasma cells make excess free light chains
  • Which are filtered
  • Overwhelm proximal tubular reabsorption and precipitate with uromodulin (Tamm–Horsfall protein) in the distal tubule
  • Forming casts that block tubules and cause inflammation.
Other renal mechanisms in myelomaHypercalcaemia (dehydration, vasoconstriction), dehydration, NSAIDs for bone pain, contrast, AL amyloid (nephrotic syndrome), light-chain deposition disease, Fanconi syndrome, infection.
Suspect in AKI with anaemia, bone pain, hypercalcaemia, high ESR/total protein, recurrent infections, or "CRAB" (Calcium high, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions).
DiagnosisDetail
Serum free light chains (kappa:lambda ratio)Very high involved light chain; key urgent test
Serum protein electrophoresis + immunofixationParaprotein (M-band)
Urine (Bence Jones protein)Note: dipstick misses light chains (detects albumin)
FBC, calcium, ESR, β2-microglobulin, albuminAnaemia, staging
Imaging: whole-body MRI or low-dose CTLytic lesions
Bone marrow biopsy (≥10% clonal plasma cells); renal biopsy if unclearConfirm
  • Management: urgent haematology/renal input
    • IV fluids (aim ~3 L urine/day)
    • stop nephrotoxins
    • treat hypercalcaemia (fluids, bisphosphonate)
    • rapid chemotherapy to cut light chains (bortezomib + dexamethasone-based)
    • dialysis if needed
    • later autologous stem cell transplant if fit.

los.text: Identify the role of renin angiotensin system in initiation and progression of kidney damage.
los.html:
• Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, keeping glomerular pressure and GFR up when perfusion falls.
RoleEffect
In hypovolaemia / low perfusion
  • Efferent constriction maintains GFR
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs remove this → GFR falls (worse with NSAIDs, which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation: "triple whammy" with diuretics)
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis
In chronic kidney damageSustained glomerular hypertension → hyperfiltration, proteinuria, podocyte injury, glomerulosclerosis; angiotensin II and aldosterone drive inflammation and fibrosis (TGF-β)
Treatment
  • ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria → slow CKD progression (diabetic nephropathy, proteinuric CKD)
  • SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone add protection
  • Practical: after starting an ACE inhibitor/ARB, check U&E in 1–2 weeks
    • a creatinine rise <30% (eGFR fall <25%) is acceptable
    • stop temporarily during AKI or dehydrating illness.

los.text: Select different tests to assess causes and severity of renal failure.
los.html:
TestPurpose
U&E (creatinine, urea, K⁺) vs baseline; VBG (pH, bicarbonate)Diagnosis, staging, dangerous hyperkalaemia and acidosis
Urine dipstick (before catheterisation)Blood + protein → glomerulonephritis; leucocytes/nitrites → infection
Urine ACR/PCR, microscopyProteinuria; red cell casts (GN), muddy brown granular casts (ATN)
FBC + film, LDH, haptoglobinAnaemia, thrombocytopenia with fragments (HUS/TTP)
CKRhabdomyolysis
CRP, cultures, LFT, calcium, bone profileSepsis, myeloma, liver disease
Renal ultrasound (within 24 h if obstruction suspected or no clear cause)Hydronephrosis; small kidneys = CKD
Immunology: ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, dsDNA, complement (C3, C4), ASO; myeloma screen; hepatitis B/C, HIVIntrinsic causes
Renal biopsyUnexplained intrinsic AKI
  • Severity: KDIGO stage, K⁺, pH/bicarbonate, fluid overload (pulmonary oedema), urine output, uraemic complications.
  • eGFR is unreliable in AKI (assumes steady state).

los.text: Describe the ways in which drugs can damage the kidneys and the adjustments necessary when dosing a patient with impaired kidney function
los.html:
MechanismDrugs
Reduced renal perfusion (pre-renal)NSAIDs (afferent constriction), ACE inhibitors/ARBs (efferent dilatation), diuretics (hypovolaemia), calcineurin inhibitors
Acute tubular necrosisAminoglycosides (gentamicin), vancomycin, iodinated contrast, amphotericin, cisplatin
Acute interstitial nephritis (allergic: rash, fever, eosinophilia)PPIs, penicillins, NSAIDs, rifampicin, diuretics
Crystal nephropathyAciclovir, methotrexate
Glomerular / otherGold, penicillamine (nephrotic); lithium (diabetes insipidus, CKD)
  • Dosing in impaired renal function: renally cleared drugs accumulate:
DrugAdjustment
MetforminReview if eGFR <45, stop if <30 (lactic acidosis); stop in AKI
Gentamicin, vancomycinDose by weight and CrCl; levels
LMWH (enoxaparin)Reduce dose if CrCl <30
DOACsDose by CrCl (avoid at low CrCl)
Digoxin, lithiumLower dose, levels
Morphine, codeine, gabapentin/pregabalinReduce or switch (oxycodone, fentanyl)
NitrofurantoinAvoid if eGFR <45
Sulfonylureas, insulinHypoglycaemia risk
  • Use the BNF renal impairment section and Renal Drug Handbook; use creatinine clearance for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.

los.text: Recall the basic steps of identification and management of AKI.
los.html:
• Recognise: e-alert, KDIGO criteria, compare with baseline.
  • STOP approach:
StepAction
SepsisLook for and treat infection (Sepsis Six)
ToxinsStop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics, metformin, gentamicin); adjust doses
Optimise volume and BPAssess fluid status; IV fluid bolus (e.g. 500 mL crystalloid, reassess) if hypovolaemic; stop antihypertensives if hypotensive
Prevent harm
  • Treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload
  • Urine dip, fluid balance, daily weights, U&E daily
  • Catheter for retention
  • Renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
Indications for renal replacement therapy("AEIOU")Refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxication (lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate), refractory fluid Overload (pulmonary oedema), Uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy).
Refer to nephrologyStage 3, suspected glomerulonephritis or intrinsic disease, no improvement, need for RRT; urology for obstruction.
After AKICheck U&E, medicines reconciliation, restart drugs carefully, discharge summary with AKI stage and advice; risk of later CKD.

los.text: Interpret urea and electrolytes (U&Es) results and determine the likely cause of any derangements
los.html:
AnalyteTypical rangeRaisedLow
Sodium135–145 mmol/LWater loss (dehydration, diabetes insipidus)See ICM Year 2 › Renal & urology › LO 2
Potassium3.5–5.3 mmol/LAKI/CKD, drugs, acidosis, haemolysed sampleDiuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea
Urea2.5–7.8 mmol/LDehydration, AKI, upper GI bleed, high protein intake, steroidsLiver failure, malnutrition, pregnancy
Creatinine~60–110 µmol/L (muscle mass dependent)Reduced GFRLow muscle mass (elderly, amputees)
eGFR>90 mL/min/1.73 m²<60 for 3 months = CKD
  • Approach: compare with baseline
    • look at the pattern: high urea out of proportion to creatinine → pre-renal or GI bleed
    • high K⁺ with high creatinine → AKI/CKD
    • low Na⁺ → check volume status and drugs
    • correlate with the drug chart, fluid balance and history
    • repeat if the sample may be haemolysed.

los.text: Identify and classify different conditions that can cause U&E imbalances (e.g., renal failure, dehydration, endocrine disorders)
los.html:
DerangementCauses
Hyponatraemia, hypovolaemicVomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics (thiazides), Addison's, burns
Hyponatraemia, euvolaemicSIADH (pneumonia, small-cell lung cancer, CNS disease, drugs: SSRIs, carbamazepine), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, psychogenic polydipsia
Hyponatraemia, hypervolaemicHeart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD
HypernatraemiaWater loss or poor intake (frail elderly), diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis (hyperglycaemia), excess saline
Hyperkalaemia
  • AKI/CKD, drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, amiloride, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, heparin), Addison's, DKA/acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, blood transfusion
  • Spurious (haemolysis, delayed sample, high WCC/platelets)
HypokalaemiaLoop/thiazide diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), Cushing's, insulin, salbutamol, refeeding, hypomagnesaemia
Raised urea and creatininePre-renal (dehydration), renal, post-renal AKI; CKD
  • Endocrine clues: Addison's = low Na⁺ + high K⁺ (+ hypotension, pigmentation); Conn's = hypertension + low K⁺.

los.text: List and evaluate management strategies for correcting U&E derangements based on the underlying cause and clinical presentation
los.html:
ProblemManagement
Severe hyperkalaemia (K⁺ ≥6.5 or ECG changes)
  • Cardiac monitor
  • IV calcium gluconate 10% (30 mL; or calcium chloride 10 mL) to stabilise the myocardium
  • Insulin 10 units (soluble) with 25 g glucose IV to shift K⁺ into cells (monitor glucose)
  • Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg
  • Treat the cause, stop culprit drugs
  • K⁺ binder (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer)
  • Dialysis if refractory
Hypokalaemia
  • Oral K⁺ if mild (e.g. Sando-K)
  • IV KCl in sodium chloride if <2.5 or symptomatic, no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally (higher only with cardiac monitoring)
  • Check and correct magnesium
  • Treat the cause
Hyponatraemia: hypovolaemic0.9% sodium chloride; stop thiazides
Hyponatraemia: SIADHTreat cause, fluid restriction (e.g. 1 L/day); tolvaptan (specialist)
Hyponatraemia: hypervolaemicFluid restriction, treat heart failure/cirrhosis (diuretics)
Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, reduced GCS)Hypertonic (2.7–3%) saline bolus in HDU; senior input
Rate of correctionSodium rise ≤10 mmol/L in 24 h (≤8 if high risk: alcohol, malnutrition) to avoid osmotic demyelination
HypernatraemiaReplace water (oral, or 5% glucose IV), correct slowly
Dehydration/pre-renal AKIIV crystalloid boluses, reassess, maintenance fluids

los.text: Perform a DRABC assessment on a sick child in line with the Resus Council UK Guidelines
los.html:
• DRABC (Resuscitation Council UK paediatric BLS):
StepAction
DangerCheck it's safe
ResponseStimulate and ask loudly "Are you all right?" (don't shake if spinal injury possible); shout for help
AirwayHead tilt, chin lift: neutral position in infants, "sniffing" in older children; jaw thrust if trauma
BreathingLook, listen, feel ≤10 s; if not breathing normally give 5 rescue breaths (mouth to mouth-and-nose in infants)
Circulation
  • No signs of life → chest compressions 15:2
  • Depth at least one third of the chest (~4 cm infant, ~5 cm child), rate 100–120/min
  • Infants: two thumbs encircling (or two fingers)
Call
  • Emergency services (phone on speaker)
  • If alone with no phone, do 1 minute of CPR first
  • Attach an AED when available
  • Sick child (not arrested): A–E with paediatric observation ranges and PEWS:
AgeHR (bpm)RR (/min)
<1 year110–16030–40
1–2 years100–15025–35
2–5 years95–14025–30
5–12 years80–12020–25
>12 years60–10015–20
  • Useful numbers: estimated weight (APLS) (age + 4) × 2 for 1–5 years
    • fluid bolus 10 mL/kg crystalloid (reassess)
    • hypoglycaemia: 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose.

los.text: Manage a sick child through collaboration and teamwork between nursing and medical students
los.html:
Collaborative management of a sick child
  • a clear team leader (stands back, keeps overview)
  • Roles allocated (airway/breathing, circulation and access, drugs and fluids, scribe/timekeeper, family support)
  • A–E with interventions as you go
  • Closed-loop communication
  • Regular summaries ("Can I recap…")
  • Escalation (paediatric registrar, PICU, 2222 paediatric emergency) with SBAR.
Nursing contributionPEWS and observations, recognising deterioration, family communication, medication checks and administration, documentation.
Debrief afterwards: what went well, what to improve.

los.text: Work together as a team recognising roles and skills of respective disciplines (nursing and medicine)
los.html:
DisciplineTypical skills and roles
NursingContinuous observation and early recognition of deterioration (PEWS/NEWS2), holistic and family-centred care, medicine administration and double checks, care planning, patient advocacy, documentation
MedicineDiagnosis, clinical reasoning, prescribing, procedures, investigations, management plans, leadership in emergencies
SharedA–E assessment, BLS, communication with family, safety checks, escalation
  • Effective teams: mutual respect
    • knowing each other's roles and limits
    • shared mental model
    • speaking up (any member can raise concerns regardless of seniority)
    • task allocation by skill
    • mutual support.

los.text: Demonstrate effective communication between nursing and medical students – consideration of body language, eye contact, direct verbal cues and responses
los.html:
Non-verbalOpen posture, eye contact, nodding, facing the person, calm tone, appropriate proximity; notice others' body language (stress, uncertainty).
Verbal
  • Address people by name
  • Clear direct instructions
  • Closed-loop ("Give 10 mL/kg saline" → "Giving 10 mL/kg saline" → "Done")
  • Check understanding
  • SBAR for handover and escalation.
Speaking upGraded assertiveness (e.g. PACE: Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency; or CUS: "I'm Concerned, I'm Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue").
Active listening and acknowledging contributions; avoid jargon and talking over each other in emergencies.

los.text: Prescribe medications safely and accurately on an inpatient drug chart, adhering to legal and institutional requirements
los.html:
Inpatient chart essentials
  • Patient details on every page: name, DOB, hospital number
  • Weight (and height)
  • Allergies box completed (drug and reaction, or "no known drug allergies")
Approved (generic) name in capitals; brand only where it matters (e.g. MR preparations, insulin, inhalers)
Dose: units in full (micrograms, units); no trailing zero (5 mg, not 5.0 mg); leading zero for decimals (0.5 mg)
Route, frequency/times, start date, indication
Antibiotics: indication and review or stop date
PRN: indication, dose, minimum interval, maximum in 24 h
Signature, printed name, bleep/contact; legible; cancel with a line, date and initials
Other chartsOnce-only and stat doses, IV fluid chart, insulin chart, anticoagulant chart; VTE assessment and prophylaxis.
CheckAllergies, interactions, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, dose against the BNF.

los.text: Calculate creatinine clearance using standard clinical formulae to inform safe drug dosing
los.html:
Cockcroft–Gault equationCrCl (mL/min) = [(140 − age) × weight (kg) × constant] ÷ serum creatinine (µmol/L), where constant = 1.23 (men), 1.04 (women).
Worked example
  • Man
  • 70 years
  • 70 kg
  • Creatinine 120 µmol/L → (70 × 70 × 1.23) ÷ 120 = 6027 ÷ 120 ≈ 50 mL/min.
WeightActual body weight usually; consider ideal or adjusted body weight in obesity (local guidance).
When to use CrCl rather than eGFRDosing narrow-therapeutic-index or renally cleared drugs (DOACs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, LMWH, digoxin, lithium), and patients at extremes of weight, the elderly. eGFR (CKD-EPI) is for staging CKD.
Neither is reliable in AKI (creatinine not at steady state).

los.text: Identify and interpret reliable resources (e.g., BNF, renal drug handbook, local guidelines) to support renal-adjusted drug prescribing
los.html:
ResourceUse
BNF (renal impairment section of each drug monograph)Dose adjustment thresholds
Renal Drug HandbookDetailed dosing by GFR and in dialysis
SPC (electronic medicines compendium)Manufacturer's licensed dosing
Local guidelines (antimicrobial app, e.g. Microguide)Gentamicin and vancomycin dosing calculators, levels
Ward pharmacist / renal pharmacistComplex cases
Nephrology teamDialysis patients
  • Interpret with the clinical picture: renal function trend (AKI vs stable CKD), weight, dialysis, drug toxicity risk; document the reasoning.

los.text: Apply local antimicrobial prescribing guidelines to select appropriate empirical treatment for urosepsis
los.html:
• Urosepsis: sepsis from a urinary source (pyelonephritis, obstructed infected kidney, catheter-associated infection, prostatitis).
StepDetail
Sepsis Six within 1 hCultures (blood and urine) before antibiotics, lactate, fluids, oxygen, urine output
CheckAllergies, previous urine cultures (ESBL or other resistant organisms), renal function, pregnancy, catheter
Empirical antibiotic per local guideline
  • Commonly IV gentamicin (single daily dose by weight and CrCl, with levels) with amoxicillin, or co-amoxiclav ± gentamicin, a cephalosporin, or piperacillin–tazobactam
  • Meropenem if ESBL history
Source controlUltrasound for obstruction → urgent nephrostomy or stent; change long-term catheter
Review at 48–72 hSwitch to an oral agent guided by sensitivities (e.g. cefalexin, co-amoxiclav, trimethoprim, ciprofloxacin); total ~7–14 days
  • In AKI: aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic: use a single dose and check levels, or choose an alternative; adjust doses for CrCl.

los.text: Recognise the parts of the elbow joint with respect to bones and connective tissues.
los.html:
• Elbow joint: synovial hinge, three articulations in one capsule:
ArticulationBonesMovement
Humero-ulnarTrochlea of humerus + trochlear notch of ulnaFlexion/extension (main stability)
Humero-radialCapitulum + radial headFlexion/extension, rotation
Superior radio-ulnarRadial head + radial notch of ulna (annular ligament)Pronation/supination
Connective tissue
  • Capsule (thin front and back, thick at the sides)
  • Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament (medial epicondyle → coronoid and olecranon; resists valgus)
  • Radial (lateral) collateral ligament (lateral epicondyle → annular ligament)
  • Annular ligament
  • Fat pads
  • Olecranon bursa.
Carrying angleThe forearm angles outwards ~10–15° in extension (greater in women).
SurfaceMedial and lateral epicondyles and the olecranon form a straight line in extension and a triangle in flexion (disturbed in dislocation, not in supracondylar fracture).

los.text: Demonstrate the movements of flexion and extension at the elbow joint, identifying the muscles involved whilst summarising their main attachments and somatic nervous innervation
los.html:
MovementMusclesMain attachmentsNerve (root)
FlexionBrachialis (main flexor)Front of lower humerus → coronoid process and ulnar tuberosityMusculocutaneous (C5–6)
Biceps brachiiLong head: supraglenoid tubercle; short head: coracoid → radial tuberosity + bicipital aponeurosisMusculocutaneous (C5–6)
BrachioradialisLateral supracondylar ridge → radial styloidRadial (C5–6)
Pronator teres, forearm flexorsMedial epicondyleMedian
ExtensionTriceps brachiiLong head: infraglenoid tubercle; lateral and medial heads: back of humerus → olecranonRadial (C6–8, mainly C7)
AnconeusLateral epicondyle → olecranonRadial
ReflexesBiceps C5–6, brachioradialis C5–6, triceps C7.
TestsFlexion against resistance with forearm supinated (biceps), mid-prone (brachioradialis); extension against resistance (triceps).

los.text: Define the boundaries of the cubital fossa and the relationships of the structures therein.
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
SuperiorLine between the medial and lateral epicondyles
LateralBrachioradialis
MedialPronator teres
FloorBrachialis, supinator
RoofDeep fascia + bicipital aponeurosis; superficially the median cubital vein
Contents, lateral → medial ("Really Need Beer To Be At My Nicest")
  • Radial nerve (under brachioradialis, splitting into superficial and deep)
  • Biceps Tendon
  • Brachial Artery (dividing into radial and ulnar near the apex)
  • Median Nerve.
Clinical
  • The bicipital aponeurosis protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venepuncture of the median cubital vein
  • Supracondylar fractures can damage the brachial artery and median nerve
  • BP cuff stethoscope over the brachial artery here.

los.text: Locate the muscles biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis, triceps brachii and anconeus, and describe them as muscle groups as defined by fascial compartments, and recognise the functional significance of these groups.
los.html:
CompartmentMusclesNerveMain action
Anterior (flexor)Biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialisMusculocutaneousElbow flexion, supination (biceps), shoulder flexion and adduction (coracobrachialis)
Posterior (extensor)Triceps brachii, anconeusRadialElbow extension
Separated by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa from the humerus to the deep fascia.
Functional significance
  • Each compartment shares one nerve and one action, so a single nerve lesion knocks out a whole group (musculocutaneous: weak flexion and supination, partly covered by brachioradialis and pronator teres; radial in the axilla: lost triceps).
  • Closed compartments can develop compartment syndrome after fractures or crush.
Neurovascular bundleBrachial artery, median and ulnar nerves run in the medial bicipital groove between the compartments.

los.text: Trace the origins, courses and distributions of the major arteries and their branches that supply the shoulder, arm and forearm in relation to common sites of injury.
los.html:
1. Subclavian arteryOver the 1st rib (behind scalenus anterior).
2. Axillary artery(from the lateral border of the 1st rib)
  • 3 parts around pectoralis minor
  • Branches: superior thoracic
  • Thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic
  • Subscapular (largest), anterior and posterior circumflex humeral (round the surgical neck, with the axillary nerve).
3. Brachial artery(from the lower border of teres major)
  • Medial arm with the median nerve
  • → profunda brachii (with the radial nerve in the radial groove) and ulnar collateral branches
  • → cubital fossa.
4Divides at the neck of the radius into the radial and ulnar arteries.
5Ulnar gives the common interosseous (anterior and posterior interosseous arteries); radial and ulnar form the palmar arches.
Common injuryArtery at risk
Fractured surgical neck of humerus / shoulder dislocationPosterior circumflex humeral, axillary
Midshaft humerus fractureProfunda brachii (with radial nerve)
Supracondylar fracture (child)Brachial artery → Volkmann's ischaemic contracture
Wrist lacerationRadial, ulnar arteries

los.text: Explain the importance of anastomoses between branches of the arteries at the shoulder and in the upper limb
los.html:
Scapular anastomosisBranches of the subclavian (suprascapular, dorsal scapular / transverse cervical) join branches of the axillary (subscapular, circumflex scapular) around the scapula.
SignificanceIf the axillary artery or distal subclavian is blocked or tied between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery, blood still reaches the arm through this anastomosis.
Elbow anastomosis
  • Superior and inferior ulnar collateral and radial collateral branches of the brachial and profunda brachii join recurrent branches of the radial and ulnar arteries
  • Keeps the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is tied below the profunda brachii, and around the flexed elbow.
HandSuperficial and deep palmar arches join radial and ulnar supplies (Allen's test before radial cannulation).
General pointAnastomoses allow collateral circulation after slow occlusion, but not enough after sudden blockage.

los.text: Demonstrate the locations at which the pulses in the brachial, radial and ulnar arteries may be located.
los.html:
PulseWhere
BrachialMedial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa (and along the medial bicipital groove, pressing onto the humerus)
RadialWrist, lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon on the distal radius; also in the anatomical snuffbox
UlnarWrist, lateral to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, proximal to the pisiform (harder to feel)
  • Uses: brachial for BP and infants
    • radial for rate, rhythm, ABG and arterial lines
    • check radial-radial delay (subclavian stenosis, aortic dissection, coarctation).

los.text: Describe the courses of the main veins of the upper limb; classify and contrast the functions of the deep and superficial veins
los.html:
Superficial veinsDeep veins
PositionIn subcutaneous tissue, independent of arteriesPaired venae comitantes with the arteries (radial, ulnar, brachial) → axillary vein
Main veins
  • Cephalic (lateral: dorsal network → lateral forearm → deltopectoral groove → axillary vein)
  • Basilic (medial: pierces deep fascia mid-arm → joins brachial veins to form the axillary vein)
  • Median cubital (joins them across the cubital fossa)
Brachial veins → axillary → subclavian
FunctionHeat loss, carry blood from the skin, drain into deep veins via perforatorsCarry most of the return; pumped by muscle contraction
ValvesPresentPresent
  • Clinical: superficial veins are used for access and fistulas
    • deep vein thrombosis of the arm (axillary-subclavian) happens with central lines or effort (Paget–Schroetter).

los.text: Recognise the common sites of venous access (with key relations).
los.html:
SiteKey relations
Median cubital vein (antecubital fossa)Lies on the bicipital aponeurosis, which separates it from the brachial artery and median nerve
Cephalic vein at the wrist ("houseman's vein")Superficial radial nerve runs alongside
Dorsal venous network of the handFew structures at risk; good for cannulas
Basilic veinMedial cutaneous nerve of the forearm nearby; used for PICC lines
Internal jugular / subclavian (central)Carotid artery, pleura (pneumothorax), brachial plexus
  • Arteriovenous fistula for dialysis: radial artery to cephalic vein at the wrist (Brescia–Cimino) or brachial to cephalic at the elbow.
  • Avoid: inner wrist (radial artery, median nerve) and limbs with lymphoedema or a fistula.

los.text: Explain the relationship between venous and lymphatic drainage channels.
los.html:
• Lymph follows veins: superficial lymphatics run with the superficial veins, deep lymphatics with the deep veins.
Lymph fromRuns withNodes
Medial hand, ulnar fingers, medial forearmBasilic veinSupratrochlear (cubital) nodes above the medial epicondyle → axillary
Lateral hand, thumb, lateral forearmCephalic veinAxillary (lateral group), some to infraclavicular (deltopectoral) nodes
Deep tissuesDeep veinsAxillary nodes
All upper limb lymph reaches the axillary nodesSubclavian lymph trunk → venous angle.
Clinical
  • Hand infections give red streaks along the veins (lymphangitis) and tender epitrochlear or axillary nodes
  • Axillary node clearance → arm lymphoedema.

los.text: Identify and side a radius, and identify its main anatomical landmarks.
los.html:
• Radius (lateral, thumb side).
PartLandmarks
ProximalDisc-shaped head (articulates with capitulum and ulna), neck, radial tuberosity (biceps)
ShaftInterosseous border (medial, sharp), pronator teres roughness (lateral, midshaft)
DistalWider end; radial styloid (lateral, brachioradialis), dorsal (Lister's) tubercle (EPL turns round it), ulnar notch, carpal surface (scaphoid, lunate)
SidingHead at the top; styloid points to the thumb side; Lister's tubercle on the back; interosseous border faces the ulna.
FracturesRadial head (fall on outstretched hand), Colles' (distal radius, dorsal displacement), Smith's (volar), Galeazzi (shaft + distal radio-ulnar dislocation).

los.text: Identify and side an ulna, and identify its main anatomical landmarks.
los.html:
• Ulna (medial, little-finger side).
PartLandmarks
ProximalOlecranon (triceps), coronoid process (brachialis), trochlear notch, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity, supinator crest
ShaftInterosseous border (lateral, sharp); posterior border subcutaneous
DistalSmall head, ulnar styloid (medial, back)
SidingHook-shaped upper end; trochlear notch faces forwards; radial notch on the lateral side.
FracturesOlecranon (fall on the elbow, triceps pulls it apart), Monteggia (ulnar shaft + radial head dislocation), nightstick (isolated shaft, defending a blow).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the superior radio-ulnar joints.
los.html:
Superior (proximal) radio-ulnar joint
  • Synovial pivot: the radial head turns within a ring formed by the radial notch of the ulna (1/5) and the annular ligament (4/5), lined with cartilage
  • Shares the elbow joint capsule and cavity.
MovementPronation and supination (with the inferior radio-ulnar joint); the radius rotates around the ulna.
MusclesSupinator, biceps (supination); pronator teres, pronator quadratus (pronation).
Clinical
  • Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow): a sudden pull on a toddler's arm slips the radial head partly out of the annular ligament
  • Reduced by supination and flexion.
  • Radial head fractures block rotation.
